messages.subject: different detection mode, song and call vs. flush, meadowlark,
messages.subject_clean: different detection mode, song and call vs. flush, meadowlark,
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,
I am trying to obtain density estimates for wintering meadowlarks
(Sturnella magna)in grasslands. When collecting data, I also recorded the
mode of detection (flush, song, or call)(These birds do sing even in
winter, and vocalizations can often be heard from 200 or more meters
away). Regardless of truncation distance, intervals, or model, I was not
able to get any reasonable fit to the data (probability of greater chi-
square value was below 0.000). However, when I fit a model to data from
flushed birds only, I was able to get a reasonable fit (probability of
greater chi-square value ~0.40). Most (~75% of my detections are from
flushes, and most (also ~75%) of my vocalization detections are further
from the line, near 100m or so. Normal truncation distance is around 140
meters regardless of which data sets are used.

What I am thinking of doing is ignoring singing and calls and using
density estimates from the flush data only. I have good sample size even
without using vocalizations, and using flushes only should avoid potential
bias that may arise if the sexes vocalize at different rates. My question
is, if all else were equal (including vocalization rates between sexes)
would excluding one type of detection from my data affect my density
estimates and how? For the record, I don't feel it would because all birds
should have an equal probability of being flushed (equal detection
probability).

I have a feeling I've seen similar discussions in the archives, but have
had no luck in re-finding them. If you are aware of any, please just point
me in the right direction and sorry for the trouble.

Thank you for any help you can give.

Sincerely,
Joe Roberts
Department of Zoology
Univ. of Oklahoma

messages.subject: Re: different detection mode, song and call vs. flush,
messages.subject_clean: different detection mode, song and call vs. flush,
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joe, List,

I think the answer is "it depends".  Recall that, for distance sampling to work,
you need all animals on (and very close to) the line or at the point to be certain
to be detected.  If all birds on your lines are certain to be flushed, and
recorded as flushed, then you should get no bias by excluding the other types of
detections.  However, if a proportion of these birds sing or call before flushing
and so are recorded in the other categories, then by excluding them you will be
excluding some animals on (and very close to) the line, so you will underestimate
density.  Sounds from your message that perhaps this is not the case (75% of
vocalizations are from near 100m or so) - i.e. that they flush from the line
before they call -- but you'll know better than me.

I guess the problem with using pooled data is that you have very different
detection functions for the three types of detection (or you may be able to
combine song and call).  This can cause a pooled detection function that looks
like the one in Figure 2.1 of Buckland et al. (1993) (I don't have the newer book
to hand), i.e., with a "spike" close to 0 distance, which is hard to get a
satisfatory fit to.  Have you tried fitting type of detection as a factor
covariate in the MCDS engine?  Also, if you have enough data, you could try post-
stratifying by call type and so fitting an independent detection function to each
type; you'd then want to sum the post-stratum density estimates to get the overall
estimate.  If this still gives you trouble, send me a sample project (use File |
Export Project... and save as a zip file first) and I'll have a look at it.

Note that it doesn't matter whether all birds have an equal probability of being
flushed or not.  Distance sampling doesn't assume equal detection probability --
just that all animals on the line or point are detected.  For reliable inference
we also want the detection probability to be 1 for some distance from the line or
point (shape criterion) and a smoothly non-increasing detection function with
increasing distance.  So long as, given distance from the line, detection
probabilities are not too heterogeneous, then the pooling robustness property of
the detection function models we use mean that we get no, or very little, bias.

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--

messages.subject: Question on pooling data
messages.body_plain:
To DISTANCE users:

I am unsure what is the best way to pool my data, I have line transect data
from annual game counts over several years, with repetitions, and through
diverse vegetation types. Any advice would be very helpful....

My data set:

7 years (with 8-16 repetitions per year) of data of observations of 14
ungulate species along 8 line-transects through various amounts of 11
vegetation types.

I wish to find the long-term average density of each species per vegetation
type.

Firstly, I have analysed the data by pooling all the transects for all the
years and repetitions and stratifying for vegetation types. This gives me a
nice number of observations, to work out the density estimate per vegetation
type, and gives me the overall average density across the years, (which is
what I am interested in). However, I now realize the sample size is 1, and
so my variance is inaccurate - right?

Can boot-strapping solve this problem?

Could I:

  1.. Use the transects as samples and pool years and repetitions. However
not all transects pass through all the vegetation types, and some vegetation
types are crossed by a single transect.
  2.. Pool all the transects and repetitions and use the years as samples,
stratifying for vegetation. However the number of observations will drop and
probably be too low in the smaller vegetation areas.
 I would then need the average density per strata across the years /
transects, and if I took the mean density, would I lose the confidence
intervals anyway?

Thank you in advance, for any help. My email address is jj...@kent.ac.uk I
will be summarise any relevant replies and post them on the message board.

Julian Easton.

messages.subject: Sponsorship to attend workshops
messages.body_plain:
Hi distance-sampling folks:

As most of you know, we run distance sampling training workshops in St Andrews most
years.  We always get enquiries from people who would like to attend, but who
cannot raise all the money required for travel, subsistence and the course fees.
They are therefore looking for possible sources of sponsorship.  Many of these
enquiries come from developing countries, but some are also from students in
developed countries.

We don't currently have the resources here in St Andrews to look for possible
sponsorship avenues, but it occurred to me that perhaps some of you may already
know of organizations who may potentially provide funding for training, capacity
building, etc. and which might potentially sponsor attendees.  Perhaps you were
sponsored to come on a previous workshop?  I'd be grateful if you could send me any
suggestions you have (even if tentative), and I'll compile them into a web page
which can act as a resource for future workshop attendees.

Thanks for any help you can provide.

 - Len Thomas

messages.subject: Line Transect effort and global detection function
messages.subject_clean: Line Transect effort and global detection function
messages.body_plain:
Hello List:
In my experiment, I surveyed birds on 12 treatment areas.  Each treatment area had one survey route and each route was completed 7 times each year for 3 years. I would like to calculate densities of 8 species on each route for each year, with observer as a covariate. I am using the MCDS engine. Here's my question: How do I obtain global detection functions for each species, pooling all observations from all transects across all years, and use that information to get density estimates for each transect.

I know that effort needs to be 7x the line length for a given year. One method I have tried is to set my data filter for species only. Then, in my model, I have selected all the observations (for a given species) for a year and post-stratified by each transect, yielding 12 density estimates total - one per transect. However, when I do that, the effort is not correct, so obviously the density is also wrong. In fact, I'm not even sure how effort is calculated in this case. Is this a simple matter of scaling the calculated density by the ratio of the effort (line length) used in the model by the actual line length x 7?

Is there a way to calculate a global detection function for each species, then apply that  to a dataset filtered for species, compartment, and year?

This seems like a basic operation, but I can't seem to figure out how to do it.

Thanks for any suggestions.

Todd Plummer

I am analyzing data from a Line Transect survey completed for 12 different =
lakes.  Within each lake, 6 different habitat types were sampled in propo=
rtion to the amount of habitat present in each lake.  For the 6 habitat t=
ypes, some have a large sampling effort with lots of observations and som=
e have very few observations (ie. less than 20).

A stratified design based on habitat type gives a smaller AIC (6077) than a=
n analysis based on the whole lake (6091), however the detection function=
 does not fit well for one of the habitat types (Muck, where visibility i=
s poorer than the other types).

When I apply a global detection function (model: half normal cosine 2 adjus=
tments) to all habitat types I get a density estimate for Muck habitat as=
 approximately 1.16.  When I apply the same detection function to each st=
rata (asking for a detection function estimate by strata) I get a density=
 for Muck of 3.01.  However, when I perform an analysis on ONLY the muck =
habitat type and fit different distance intervals to obtain a BETTER fit =
of the half normal cosine model, I get a density estimate of 4.51.

In this situation is it better to apply a global detection function to a st=
ratified design (stratified by stratum/habitat), or obtain detection func=
tions for each stratum, or to perform an individual survey on those habit=
ats where the global detection function doesn't appear to fit well?

I am confused as to the most correct way to analyze this data and any sugge=
stions would be greatly appreciated.

Other information: data has been grouped (post-survey) into distance interv=
als due to heaping, and truncated by 5% (ie. truncation distance is now 2=
50 cm).  Half normal cosine model is the model selected based on min. AIC=
 and # of parameters.  Observations are in clusters, there is no size bia=
s of clusters and perpendicular distance (x), therefore cluster size is e=
stimated as a mean.  On a whole lake level there is 578 observations, L =
=3D 2672 m.

Thank you for any help you can provide,

Natalie Meade

> > wrong in my calculation (perhaps units)?  Likewise, is 0.23231E-02 to be
> > read as 0.0023231?

Your interpretation is correct.  You don't give enough details to tell why
your hand-calculated value differs.

> > My second question concerns the calculation of the standard error for the
> > density estimate for transect 213 (again shown below). I surveyed this
> > 0.6km transect 6 times. The way my data are set up there is only one
> > transect (213) entry with 3.6 in the effort (line length) column. There
> > are then several observations in the corresponding observation layer. But
> > there is no obvious way that Distance can interpret this as anything more

> > error of density from observations on essentially one transect? If
> > required, can I get the variance of the density estimate by simply
> > squaring the SE from this output?

Variance in encounter rate is estimated from variation between lines, not
from variation between runs of the same line (which cannot be treated as
independent).  Your small cv for f(0) suggests that you fitted a pooled
detection function across strata, in which case the variance for this
quantity is estimated from all the distance data.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Further to Steve's message (Happy Birthday Steve, by the way):

Joe Roberts wrote:
> >Is the problem in my understanding of the E-01, or is there something
> >wrong in my calculation (perhaps units)?

The problem is in your calculation.  Instead of:

> >My observations are not in clusters, so using numbers from the output
> >below I calculated density as 9 * 0.062790 / 2(3.6) = 0.078488.

You should have
9 * 0.062790 / 2(3600 meters) = 7.8488 E-5    (ie 10x-5) birds / square meter
To convert to hectares, mutiply by 100x100=10000 and you get 0.7848, which is
exactly what Distance gave you.

> >Likewise, is 0.23231E-02 to be
> >read as 0.0023231?

Yes.

> >My second question concerns the calculation of the standard error for the
> >density estimate for transect 213 (again shown below). I surveyed this
> >0.6km transect 6 times. The way my data are set up there is only one
> >transect (213) entry with 3.6 in the effort (line length) column. There
> >are then several observations in the corresponding observation layer.

That's right -- repeats of the same transect are not new samples, so you pool
them and multiply the line length by the number of visits.

> >But
> >there is no obvious way that Distance can interpret this as anything more
> >than one transect of 3.6km length. How is Distance calculating a standard
> >error of density from observations on essentially one transect?

Yes.  I don't have the 2001 book to hand, but in there somewhere is the formula
for estimating variance in density using the delta method:
\hat(var(D)) = \hat(D)^2[ \hat(var(n))/n^2 + \hat(var(f(0))/\hat(f(0))^2]
(no cluster size component in your case).  The default option in Distance is to
estimate the var(n) from the variation in encounter rate between lines (it's
under Model Definition | Variance).  Your question is, how can it do this when
there is only one line.  Good question!  When there is only one line, it
defaults to using the second option, which is to assume that n is a Poisson
random variable, and so to set \hat(var(n))=n.  I have changed Distnace so that
it now issues a warning when it does this -- but I can't remember if I made that
change in the last release of Distance 4.1, or after that -- in which case you
won't see the warning until Distance 5 is released.

So, to match the above with the output you appended to your message:  n=9, so
\hat(var(n))=9.  Distance reports SE of encounter rate, so we need to convert
this to encounter rate.  n/L = 9/3.6 = 2.5.
\hat(var(n/L)) = \hat(var(n)/L^2) = 9/3.6^2 = 0.694
\hat(SE) = sqrt(\hat(var)) = 0.833, which is what Distance got.

I'll leave you to recreate the SE of the density estimate using the delta method
if you want.

> >If
> >required, can I get the variance of the density estimate by simply
> >squaring the SE from this output?

Yes.

Cheers,

 - Len

messages.body_plain:
Hi Natalie, List,

I was a bit confused by this bit:

On Tue, 27 Jul 2004 09:58:47 -0400, Natalie Meade wrote:
> >When I apply a global detection function (model: half normal cosine 2

adjustments) to all habitat types I get a density estimate for Muck habitat as
approximately 1.16.  When I apply the same detection function to each strata
(asking for a detection function estimate by strata) I get a density for Muck of
3.01.  However, when I perform an analysis on ONLY the muck habitat type and fit
different distance intervals to obtain a BETTER fit of the half normal cosine

model, I get a density estimate of 4.51.

In the first case, do you mean you estimated density using a global detection
function and global encounter rate, while in the second you used a global
detection function and encounter rate by stratum?  If so, the second option is
always better than the first -- i.e., it is always better to model encounter
rate at the lowest level for which you want density.

However, you were wondering about the third option -- ie detection function by
stratum and encounter rate by stratum.  You said that this gives a lower AIC for
the detection function, but that there are few observations in that one stratum
and it gives a poor fit.  It's hard to get a reliable fit with so few
detections.  Can I suggest two alternatives?

(1) you could try fitting habitat as a covariate in the MCDS engine.  In the
MCDS Model Defintion, you'd still have habitat as stratum, but you'd tick both
the detection function global and detection function by stratum boxes -- this
tells Distance to fit a global detection function but estimate f(0) by stratum.
Under Covariates, include habitat as a factor covariate.  For more on this, see
the online help, Chapter 9, under Defining MCDS models.

(2) Can you pool some habitats together; ones you expect to have similar
detection functions?

Hope this helps,

 - Len

How about the following:  set up the project with one record in the sample layer
for each route in each year -- ie 12x3=36 records.  For each record, effort is 7x
line length for the given year.  Observer is a field at the appropriate level
(sample if the same observer did all 7 repeats of a line, or observation if not.)
You also need species as a field in the observation layer.  Set up a data filter
for each species.  Set up a model definition with detection function global and
encounter rate and density by sample.  Should give you what you want.

Note that the sample density estimates will not be independent, because they share
some parameters in the detection function.  You'll need to take this into account
if you want to get variances on comparisons of densities across years or treatment
areas (unless they share the same observer, in which case you're effectively just
comparing encounter rates).  Probably conceptually the simplest way to do this is
to bootstrap the comparison.  E.g., if you want to compare density in the first
and last year then calculate the difference in density, draw a bootstrap resample
from your data (at whatever level is appropriate -- are treatment areas the random
thing here?), refit the data in Distance (probably calling the MCDS engine
directly from whatever program you use to do the bootstrap) calculate a new
difference, repeat many times and this gives you and estimate of the distribution
of the differences.  Downside is that you have to program in some language to do
this.

Finally, thanks for sending me your project file (under separate cover) - I hope
the above answers your questions.  However, can I please implore everyone who
wants to send a project file to me to export it as a zip file first -- read the
online manual, Chapter 4 for details.

Cheers,

 - Len

You can get the equivalent of what you want (scaled by 2w) if you
specify a uniform key with no adjustments.  That will analyse the data
as a strip transect and the individual density estimates are simply the
encounter rates divided by 2w.  Not sure why you are doing what you are
doing though.

messages.subject: Re: grouping of heaped data
messages.body_plain:
> > Another question for the list.  Concerning grouping of data to reduce the effects of heaping, can someone please explain to me the general method of doing this in Distance?  I'm not sure when I'm selecting my group cut-points if I'm aiming for the best fit of the groups to the detection function of an arbitrarily picked model, or if I should be using the GOF test values for the cutpoints to obtain groupings that have the lowest Chi-square value?
> >
> > In some cases, when I have a very low Chi-square value for my first interval, the group has a detection probability that is not very close to 1 (ie. 0.85, 0.9).  In other cases, I will have a first interval group that has a detection probability very close to 1, however the chi-square value for that interval is higher than the former example.
> >
> > How does one decide what the best grouping is to reduce the effects of heaping?  I can't seem to find a definitive answer in the manual/book.

I would not choose intervals with reference to goodness-of-fit statistics
- though a good choice of groups should improve the reliability of gof
tests.  I would examine the data, and the behaviour of my observers, to
determine what the favoured rounding distances are.  I would then choose
cutpoints to try to ensure that these favoured distances fall well away
from cutpoints.  In this way, few observations should end up in the wrong
group.

If heaping is substantial, I would also look to improve field methods and
observer training, and assess whether technology such as survey lasers can
reduce the problem of heaping.

Steve Buckland
